Summary
Support
Supporters argue that the people who would pay the tax are the ones who benefited the most financially from recent federal tax reforms. Congress also cut tens of billions from Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, which provides health insurance to low-income people. SEIU-UHW argues those cuts will cause hospitals and clinics to close, costing thousands of jobs and worsening access for all patients.
Oppose
Opponents include Silicon Valley entrepreneurs, business interests, and some health and labor organizations. They say the proposal will backfire, causing billionaires to leave California and decreasing tax revenue in the long run. Health groups say they weren’t consulted in designing the measure and that it does not solve the long-term fiscal challenges of funding healthcare. The same groups backed propositions 41 and 42, competing measures that would place limits on new special taxes.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . # Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California.*** Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property.
These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate.
One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year.
Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
...
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
...
### Fiscal Effect
***Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future.*** Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future.
This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.
This could reduce future tax revenues.
When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

Proposition 42 would add a new article to the California Constitution with two main provisions:
- First, it would prohibit any new taxes on personal property—both tangible (i.e., personal belongings) and intangible (savings, retirement accounts, financial assets, business ownership, intellectual property, etc.)—while leaving existing property taxes untouched.

Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California.*** Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property.
These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate.
One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year.
Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
***Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.*** The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California.*** Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property.
These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate.
One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year.
Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
***Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.*** The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

# What Would Proposition 42 Mean for California?
Understanding the Prohibition on Taxing Certain Assets and Enacting Retroactive Taxes
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson
...
Prop.
42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of certain assets as well as taxes that apply retroactively.
The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop.
40 — the one-time billionaire tax measure also appearing on the November ballot — if it receives more votes, and it would also create new barriers to raising progressive state revenue in the future to adequately meet the needs of Californians.
...
Prop.
42 would amend the state Constitution to prohibit taxes on the ownership of certain assets and on certain retroactive taxes.
### Prohibition on New Taxes on Assets
Prop.
42 would prohibit the imposition of any new state tax — enacted on or after January 1, 2026 — on the ownership of financial assets (such as bank accounts, stocks, bonds, or mutual funds), retirement accounts, interests in businesses, intellectual property, and other personal property (such as vehicles, jewelry, artwork, and other movable, physical property).
### Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Prop.
42 would prohibit the imposition of new retroactive taxes, specifically any tax that is based on “conduct, activities, or a status” that preceded the effective date of the tax.
The measure also explicitly prohibits taxes based on someone’s residency status prior to the tax going into effect.

# Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure

Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026.
It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.

Issue Brief
What Would Proposition 42 Mean for California?
Understanding the Prohibition on Taxing Certain Assets and Enacting Retroactive Taxes
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of certain assets as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the one-time billionaire tax measure also appearing on the November ballot — if it receives more votes, and it would also create new barriers to raising progressive state revenue in the future to adequately meet the needs of Californians.
What Would Prop. 42 Do?
Prop. 42 would amend the state Constitution to prohibit taxes on the ownership of certain assets and on certain retroactive taxes.
Prohibition on New Taxes on Assets
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of any new state tax — enacted on or after January 1, 2026 — on the ownership of financial assets (such as bank accounts, stocks, bonds, or mutual funds), retirement accounts, interests in businesses, intellectual property, and other personal property (such as vehicles, jewelry, artwork, and other movable, physical property).
Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of new retroactive taxes, specifically any tax that is based on “conduct, activities, or a status” that preceded the effective date of the tax. The measure also explicitly prohibits taxes based on someone’s residency status prior to the tax going into effect. An exception would be made for retroactive taxes in cases where the revenues would be used to respond to a governor-declared emergency and the tax does not apply retroactively for more than one year before the effective date.
What Would Prop. 42 Mean for Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 42 is to invalidate Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/), which would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires. The tax would apply retroactively to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026 and would apply to financial assets like stocks and bonds and other types of assets that would put it in direct conflict with Prop. 42’s prohibition of such taxes — though Prop. 40 would exclude retirement accounts, which is a key focus of Prop. 42. If both measures were to pass and Prop. 42 received more votes, Prop. 40 would likely be invalidated.
But the measure would also have more far-reaching consequences by making it harder for state leaders to raise revenues from wealthy households to effectively meet the needs of Californians and to quickly adapt to changing circumstances.
This would come at a time when California is facing challenges on multiple fronts — the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), the sustained high poverty rate (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/poverty-in-california-remains-steady-among-the-highest-in-the-nation/), the ongoing housing affordability and homelessness crises, and rising costs of maintaining current services due to inflation and an aging population. Addressing these issues and ensuring California communities can thrive will require the state to substantially raise ongoing revenues (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
While Prop. 42 would reduce the options state policymakers have to increase revenues, California voters may still be able to amend the state Constitution in the future to allow a new tax on assets or one that applied retroactively. However, legal challenges are possible and there is no absolute certainty on how courts would rule.
Impacts of Prohibition on Taxing Assets
Currently, the ownership of assets is generally not taxed in California, with the exception of local property taxes on real estate — already subject to strict constitutional limits under Prop. 13 (1978) — and some types of personal property including boats, planes, and business equipment, as well as state vehicle license fees.
While the state does not currently tax (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/#h-what-is-the-difference-between-income-and-wealth) the ownership of financial assets, business interests, or other intangible assets, it is not constitutionally barred from doing so. Prop. 42 would enshrine this prohibition in the state Constitution, which would prevent state leaders from creating wealth-based taxes in the future. This would limit the options policymakers have to raise progressive revenue to maintain and improve state services that support Californians in staying healthy, housed, and economically secure.
While most Californians hold assets in some form, such as checking or savings accounts, some types of assets are far more likely to be held by wealthy households. For example, about two-thirds of Californians in the top 25% of the wealth distribution hold stocks, bonds, or mutual funds, compared to only 9% of Californians in the bottom 25%, according to an analysis by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf).
Current federal and state tax policies allow some large wealth increases to never be taxed. California — like the federal government — only taxes the income people receive when they sell their assets, but does not tax the growth in value of assets they hold onto. This growth is known as an unrealized capital gain, and for very wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. Some wealthy people may even be able to avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis,” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year.
For these reasons, broadly prohibiting state leaders from enacting any new taxes on assets would narrow the options available to ensure that the wealthiest Californians pay their fair share to support the services that benefit residents across the state.
Impacts of Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Many federal and state tax law changes have modest retroactivity periods, such as looking back to the beginning of a tax year. This has the benefit of reducing taxpayers’ ability to engage in activities to avoid or evade the tax before it goes into effect, which would reduce the revenue potential. Looking back to the start of the current tax year can also more immediately raise revenues when there are urgent needs.

What Would Proposition 42 Mean for California?
Understanding the Prohibition on Taxing Certain Assets and Enacting Retroactive Taxes
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of certain assets as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the one-time billionaire tax measure also appearing on the November ballot — if it receives more votes, and it would also create new barriers to raising progressive state revenue in the future to adequately meet the needs of Californians.
What Would Prop. 42 Do?
Prop. 42 would amend the state Constitution to prohibit taxes on the ownership of certain assets and on certain retroactive taxes.
Prohibition on New Taxes on Assets
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of any new state tax — enacted on or after January 1, 2026 — on the ownership of financial assets (such as bank accounts, stocks, bonds, or mutual funds), retirement accounts, interests in businesses, intellectual property, and other personal property (such as vehicles, jewelry, artwork, and other movable, physical property).
Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of new retroactive taxes, specifically any tax that is based on “conduct, activities, or a status” that preceded the effective date of the tax. The measure also explicitly prohibits taxes based on someone’s residency status prior to the tax going into effect. An exception would be made for retroactive taxes in cases where the revenues would be used to respond to a governor-declared emergency and the tax does not apply retroactively for more than one year before the effective date.
What Would Prop. 42 Mean for Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 42 is to invalidate Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/), which would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires. The tax would apply retroactively to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026 and would apply to financial assets like stocks and bonds and other types of assets that would put it in direct conflict with Prop. 42’s prohibition of such taxes — though Prop. 40 would exclude retirement accounts, which is a key focus of Prop. 42. If both measures were to pass and Prop. 42 received more votes, Prop. 40 would likely be invalidated.
But the measure would also have more far-reaching consequences by making it harder for state leaders to raise revenues from wealthy households to effectively meet the needs of Californians and to quickly adapt to changing circumstances.
This would come at a time when California is facing challenges on multiple fronts — the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), the sustained high poverty rate (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/poverty-in-california-remains-steady-among-the-highest-in-the-nation/), the ongoing housing affordability and homelessness crises, and rising costs of maintaining current services due to inflation and an aging population. Addressing these issues and ensuring California communities can thrive will require the state to substantially raise ongoing revenues (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
While Prop. 42 would reduce the options state policymakers have to increase revenues, California voters may still be able to amend the state Constitution in the future to allow a new tax on assets or one that applied retroactively. However, legal challenges are possible and there is no absolute certainty on how courts would rule.
Impacts of Prohibition on Taxing Assets
Currently, the ownership of assets is generally not taxed in California, with the exception of local property taxes on real estate — already subject to strict constitutional limits under Prop. 13 (1978) — and some types of personal property including boats, planes, and business equipment, as well as state vehicle license fees.
While the state does not currently tax (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/#h-what-is-the-difference-between-income-and-wealth) the ownership of financial assets, business interests, or other intangible assets, it is not constitutionally barred from doing so. Prop. 42 would enshrine this prohibition in the state Constitution, which would prevent state leaders from creating wealth-based taxes in the future. This would limit the options policymakers have to raise progressive revenue to maintain and improve state services that support Californians in staying healthy, housed, and economically secure.
While most Californians hold assets in some form, such as checking or savings accounts, some types of assets are far more likely to be held by wealthy households. For example, about two-thirds of Californians in the top 25% of the wealth distribution hold stocks, bonds, or mutual funds, compared to only 9% of Californians in the bottom 25%, according to an analysis by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf).
Current federal and state tax policies allow some large wealth increases to never be taxed. California — like the federal government — only taxes the income people receive when they sell their assets, but does not tax the growth in value of assets they hold onto. This growth is known as an unrealized capital gain, and for very wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. Some wealthy people may even be able to avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis,” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year.
For these reasons, broadly prohibiting state leaders from enacting any new taxes on assets would narrow the options available to ensure that the wealthiest Californians pay their fair share to support the services that benefit residents across the state.
Impacts of Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Many federal and state tax law changes have modest retroactivity periods, such as looking back to the beginning of a tax year. This has the benefit of reducing taxpayers’ ability to engage in activities to avoid or evade the tax before it goes into effect, which would reduce the revenue potential. Looking back to the start of the current tax year can also more immediately raise revenues when there are urgent needs.
Broadly prohibiting retroactive taxation would hamstring the ability of state leaders to enact effective and timely tax policy changes that raise revenues needed to meet the needs of Californians.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 42?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 41 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-would-proposition-41-mean-for-california/). The measure is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Professional Firefighters, and the State Building & Construction Trades Council of California.
There is no official opposition campaign for Prop. 41, but prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU-UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters are also opposed.

These proposals haven’t advanced, and while an amendment could bar new wealth taxes, it's not an immediate concern. The term "all personal property" could imply some spillover to state taxes based on ownership.**Examining wealth tax criticisms**

I need to explore the criticisms of wealth taxes from credible sources like the OECD and Prop 40 economic studies. Issue Brief
What Would Proposition 42 Mean for California?
Understanding the Prohibition on Taxing Certain Assets and Enacting Retroactive Taxes
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of certain assets as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the one-time billionaire tax measure also appearing on the November ballot — if it receives more votes, and it would also create new barriers to raising progressive state revenue in the future to adequately meet the needs of Californians.
What Would Prop. 42 Do?
Prop. 42 would amend the state Constitution to prohibit taxes on the ownership of certain assets and on certain retroactive taxes.
Prohibition on New Taxes on Assets
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of any new state tax — enacted on or after January 1, 2026 — on the ownership of financial assets (such as bank accounts, stocks, bonds, or mutual funds), retirement accounts, interests in businesses, intellectual property, and other personal property (such as vehicles, jewelry, artwork, and other movable, physical property).
Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of new retroactive taxes, specifically any tax that is based on “conduct, activities, or a status” that preceded the effective date of the tax. The measure also explicitly prohibits taxes based on someone’s residency status prior to the tax going into effect. An exception would be made for retroactive taxes in cases where the revenues would be used to respond to a governor-declared emergency and the tax does not apply retroactively for more than one year before the effective date.
What Would Prop. 42 Mean for Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 42 is to invalidate Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/), which would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires. The tax would apply retroactively to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026 and would apply to financial assets like stocks and bonds and other types of assets that would put it in direct conflict with Prop. 42’s prohibition of such taxes — though Prop. 40 would exclude retirement accounts, which is a key focus of Prop. 42. If both measures were to pass and Prop. 42 received more votes, Prop. 40 would likely be invalidated.
But the measure would also have more far-reaching consequences by making it harder for state leaders to raise revenues from wealthy households to effectively meet the needs of Californians and to quickly adapt to changing circumstances.
This would come at a time when California is facing challenges on multiple fronts — the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), the sustained high poverty rate (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/poverty-in-california-remains-steady-among-the-highest-in-the-nation/), the ongoing housing affordability and homelessness crises, and rising costs of maintaining current services due to inflation and an aging population. Addressing these issues and ensuring California communities can thrive will require the state to substantially raise ongoing revenues (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
While Prop. 42 would reduce the options state policymakers have to increase revenues, California voters may still be able to amend the state Constitution in the future to allow a new tax on assets or one that applied retroactively. However, legal challenges are possible and there is no absolute certainty on how courts would rule.
Impacts of Prohibition on Taxing Assets
Currently, the ownership of assets is generally not taxed in California, with the exception of local property taxes on real estate — already subject to strict constitutional limits under Prop. 13 (1978) — and some types of personal property including boats, planes, and business equipment, as well as state vehicle license fees.
While the state does not currently tax (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/#h-what-is-the-difference-between-income-and-wealth) the ownership of financial assets, business interests, or other intangible assets, it is not constitutionally barred from doing so. Prop. 42 would enshrine this prohibition in the state Constitution, which would prevent state leaders from creating wealth-based taxes in the future. This would limit the options policymakers have to raise progressive revenue to maintain and improve state services that support Californians in staying healthy, housed, and economically secure.
While most Californians hold assets in some form, such as checking or savings accounts, some types of assets are far more likely to be held by wealthy households. For example, about two-thirds of Californians in the top 25% of the wealth distribution hold stocks, bonds, or mutual funds, compared to only 9% of Californians in the bottom 25%, according to an analysis by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf).
Current federal and state tax policies allow some large wealth increases to never be taxed. California — like the federal government — only taxes the income people receive when they sell their assets, but does not tax the growth in value of assets they hold onto. This growth is known as an unrealized capital gain, and for very wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. Some wealthy people may even be able to avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis,” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year.
For these reasons, broadly prohibiting state leaders from enacting any new taxes on assets would narrow the options available to ensure that the wealthiest Californians pay their fair share to support the services that benefit residents across the state.
Impacts of Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Many federal and state tax law changes have modest retroactivity periods, such as looking back to the beginning of a tax year. This has the benefit of reducing taxpayers’ ability to engage in activities to avoid or evade the tax before it goes into effect, which would reduce the revenue potential. Looking back to the start of the current tax year can also more immediately raise revenues when there are urgent needs.
Broadly prohibiting retroactive taxation would hamstring the ability of state leaders to enact effective and timely tax policy changes that raise revenues needed to meet the needs of Californians.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 42?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 41 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-would-proposition-41-mean-for-california/). The measure is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Professional Firefighters, and the State Building & Construction Trades Council of California.
There is no official opposition campaign for Prop. 41, but prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU-UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters are also opposed.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.

Prop. 41 would 1) impose new audit requirements for programs funded with state special taxes and 2) prohibit the collection of new state taxes that are excluded from the state’s spending limit. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax also appearing on the November ballot … Continued

**Analyzing tax provisions**

I'm discovering that the CalBudget Center leans towards partisan and tax-supportive analysis, but I need to dive deeper into the actual legal text, especially regarding retroactive provisions. There's a clause referring to certain provisions that apply only to laws enacted after January 1, 2026, which could close options for new taxes. I'm curious about whether "worker pensions" are defined and how the provision deals with asset ownership, particularly concerning wealth and property taxes. Would this effectively block a wealth tax? It seems so.**Evaluating wealth tax options**

I believe it’s important to preserve the wealth tax option, even if one can argue it’s not the best tool. Prop 42 appears to extend beyond just a wealth tax and may block other taxes on accumulated wealth, intellectual property, and certain personal property in the future. While the state can tax wages and transactions, it needs flexibility. I’ll need to look into the specifics of Prop 40 and its revenue use, including the timing and the mixed support behind Prop 42, though there are concerns about the funding sources.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

PROP 42: The Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-09/California%20Decides_Proposition%2042.pdf)
Research
Overview
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Proposition 42 would add a new article to the California Constitution with two main provisions:
First, it would prohibit any new taxes on personal property—both tangible (i.e., personal belongings) and intangible (savings, retirement accounts, financial assets, business ownership, intellectual property, etc.)—while leaving existing property taxes untouched. In effect, this would require that the California legislature get voters’ approval before creating any new property taxes.
Second, it would prohibit new taxes that impose liability for past residency or conduct, with a narrow exception allowing taxes to reach back up to 365 days if tied to a governor-declared emergency and dedicated to addressing it.
Notably, if Prop 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, it would nullify Prop 40 entirely. Given the two propositions fundamentally conflict, this kind of specificity is valuable to clearly determine what happens after the election. This is arguably the most relevant element of Prop 42, because Prop 40 could possibly allow future legislators to pass new taxes on personal property.
Fellows at the Hoover Institution have extensively researched (https://fiscalrealitycheck.substack.com/p/a-california-ballot-collision-wealth) Prop 40, Prop 42, and California’s fiscal problems more generally. The biggest fiscal challenge the state faces is an exuberance of spending beyond what even its rapidly increasing tax revenue can sustain.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0041A1)
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment and statute
A vote YES means: A prohibition on new state taxes on personal property, including financial assets. Retroactive taxes would be prohibited except during a state of emergency. If Proposition 42 outpolls Proposition 40, it would specifically void Prop 40 (see California Decides Proposition Lab, Prop 40: The Billionaire Tax Act (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)).
A vote NO means: The legislature would not be forbidden from passing new taxes on personal property, including financial assets. The legislature would not be forbidden from passing retroactive taxes. The lack of these restrictions is especially relevant if Proposition 40 passes, because Prop 40 arguably empowers future legislatures to pass new taxes on personal property and to create retroactive taxes.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0041A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0041A1%20(Retirement%20Protection%20).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0041 (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250545.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 40 imposes a one-time tax of 5 percent on the total net worth of any California resident worth $1 billion or more. The rate applies to the whole fortune, not just the amount above the threshold. A narrow phase-in ramps the rate between 0 percent at $1.0 billion and 5 percent at $1.1 billion. A married couple is treated as a single taxpayer.
Residency is set as of January 1, 2026, called the tax obligation date, and net worth is measured on December 31, 2026, called the valuation date. The January date is already in the past. A billionaire who leaves California before the election would still owe the tax if voters approve it because the law reaches back to who lived here on the first day of the year. The tax is due in 2027 with 2026 tax returns, payable in full or in five annual installments that carry a 7.5 percent additional charge each year.
Not all assets are included in the net worth calculation. Directly held real estate is excluded, which sidesteps a fight with Proposition 13 restrictions. Pensions and traditional retirement accounts are excluded, Roth accounts are excluded up to $10 million, and up to $5 million of art, cars, and personal property is excluded.
The revenue from this tax is not allowed to go into the general fund. The constitutional amendment routes it into a separate reserve fund that sits outside the Gann appropriations limit, the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee, and the rainy-day budget rules. The revenue is earmarked: 90 percent goes to healthcare and 10 percent to education and food assistance, with annual spending caps of $22.5 billion and $2.5 billion. This provision reaches every taxpayer in the state: All 19 million-plus California income tax filers would have to declare whether their net worth exceeds $1 billion.
2. The legal language
Full text:
Initiative 25-0041A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0041A1%20(Retirement%20Protection%20).pdf) (six pages, amended language filed January 12, 2026)
Key language:
“No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026 may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether held directly or indirectly.”
What it amends:
Adds a new Article VIII to the California Constitution. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it, and only another vote of the people can undo it. The measure borrows the definition of “tax” from Article XIII A, Section 3, the Proposition 13 and Proposition 26 definition. It also includes a conflicting-measures clause that reaches other initiatives on the same ballot.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A constitutional ban on new taxes on the ownership or control of personal property, from personal belongings and savings (including retirement accounts) to business interests and intellectual property. It would also prohibit most new retroactive state taxes, including taxes keyed to a past residency date.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution.
When?
It would apply to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026.
Why?
The proponents say California already ranks among the most heavily taxed states, that families struggle to save, and that politicians should not be able to tax the value of savings and assets people have already earned.
4. Analysis and Assessment
Proposition 42 would prohibit the legislature from enacting future taxes on personal property, broadly defined. This would be a negligible change to the status quo because the state does not currently levy taxes on tangible or intangible personal property. However, it would forestall future legislatures from taxing personal property without first getting approval from voters via ballot initiative.
The California Constitution currently permits the legislature, with a two-thirds vote, to levy taxes on all tangible and intangible personal property. The first sentence of Article XIII, Section 2, reads:
The Legislature may provide for property taxation of all forms of tangible personal property, shares of capital stock, evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest therein not exempt under any other provision of this article.
This language reflects dormant tax policy going back to the 1879 California Constitution. In the 1930s, after years of controversy and litigation over taxes on intangible assets and a sharp decrease in property tax revenues caused by delinquencies during the Great Depression, the state pivoted to implement a sales tax and a personal income tax to stabilize state tax revenue. As part of the tax policy coordination, a 1933 constitutional amendment retained the language allowing the state to tax personal property but limited taxes on many financial assets to be at most 0.4 percent of the value of the asset. Today, California’s Revenue and Taxation Code exempts all intangible assets from taxation. However, the income from intangible assets like stocks and debt instruments is taxed as ordinary income.
One argument against limiting what the legislature can tax is that the state’s tax base is already narrowly dependent on personal income taxes (see California Decides FAQ: Who Pays for California’s State Budget, and What Is It Spent On? (https://www.hoover.org/research/who-pays-californias-state-budget-and-what-it-spent)). The personal income tax has grown to provide nearly 70 percent (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-01-27/california-budget-deficit-surplus-spending-commitments) of General Fund tax revenue, compared to 38 percent for total state tax collections nationally. Research by Hoover Institution fellows Lanhee J. Chen, Lee Ohanian, and Joshua D. Rauh have described how this causes substantial volatility in the California state budget (https://www.hoover.org/research/california-state-budget-and-revenue-volatility-fiscal-health-deficit-context) because most personal income tax revenue comes from high-income and high-net-worth households and tends to fluctuate with stock market performance. For example:
During the strong stock market returns in 2021 the top 10 percent of taxpayers paid almost 90 percent of personal income tax revenue.
The top 1 percent of income tax filers typically pay 40–50 percent of personal income tax revenue.
The top 0.1 percent—just twenty-five thousand households—typically pay more than 20 percent of all personal income tax revenue.
The problem with adding new state personal property taxes, especially on intangible financial assets, is that the impact will tend to be borne by the high-income and high-net-worth households. This means that creating new property taxes wouldn’t expand the tax base—it would simply be tapping the same source of revenue that California already utilizes more than almost any other state.
Dr. Rauh’s California-specific research examining taxpayers’ response to Proposition 30 (2012) shows that high-income and high-net-worth households exhibit the highest migration response to increased taxes, meaning that new state property taxes would potentially undermine the already-precarious tax base. The departure of a significant portion of the tax base for Proposition 40’s wealth tax, even before the tax is even in effect (https://libertylensecon.substack.com/p/california-wealth-tax-npv), provides further evidence of the sensitivity of high-income and high-net-worth taxpayers to increased tax rates.
On the other hand, Proposition 42 would provide a credible commitment that the state would not create new property taxes, perhaps providing some degree of reassurance for the households most susceptible to migration, such that more will remain in the state than otherwise. That wouldn’t necessarily expand the tax base, but it would at least help prevent further erosion. Prop 42’s prohibition on retroactive taxes would likely have a similar effect.
A more relevant solution to California’s financial woes would be budget reductions to counter the recent spending explosion, as well as better management of its existing revenue streams to weather the lean times. Research by Dr. Ohanian highlights that from 2019 to 2023 California’s population declined by almost five hundred thousand people (a 1 percent decrease), but the state budget increased by more than 57 percent (31 percent after adjusting for inflation).
State personal income tax revenues surged by 55 percent in 2021 due to a soaring stock market and federal support during COVID-19, but this was followed by a 35 percent drop in 2023. The bust should have been expected given California’s previous experience, but Governor Newsom’s administration assumed that the increased revenue would be permanent and increased government spending commensurately, leading to a $175 billion swing (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-01-27/california-budget-deficit-surplus-spending-commitments) from budget surplus to deficit just two years later.
The boom-bust nature of California’s tax revenue shows the need for better methods to smooth revenues and spending over time. In particular, this will require restraining state policymakers, who have shown a proclivity for pursuing large projects and program expansions during the boom times, only to discover during the bust that discretion is the better part of spending. A comprehensive solution would require extensive tax structure reforms, but in the meantime state policymakers could reduce volatility by revisiting California’s “rainy day fund” to ensure it is fit for purpose.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 42 doesn’t change any current taxes. It effectively only adds the requirement that voters be consulted before the state creates any new property taxes. It also prohibits retroactive taxes and taxes keyed to a past residency date. This provides high-income and high-net-worth households a credible signal that California will not—without reasonable warning—tax the ownership of personal property, especially financial assets. This could help slow the out-migration that erodes the state’s narrow, top-heavy tax base.
Prop 42 also contains a clause that if it outpolls Proposition 40, it will fully nullify Prop 40. This specificity is likely preferrable to having the courts attempt to determine which elements of Prop 40 (if any) still hold if Prop 42 has greater support.
Hoover Institution research shows that California’s spending has risen far faster than inflation or population growth, and even faster than the surprising increases in tax revenue. This suggests that first California should solve its expenditures problem before trying to backfill tax revenue by tapping those households already responsible for the vast majority of income tax revenue.

The Bottom Line (https://www.cnbc.com/global-cfo-council/) California's Proposition 40: What voters need to know about billionaire wealth tax battle
Published Thu, Oct 22 2026 8:05 AM EDT Updated Thu, Oct 22 2026 12:04 PM EDT
Trevor Laurence Jockims (https://www.cnbc.com/trevor-laurence-jockims/)
WATCH LIVE (https://www.cnbc.com/live-tv/)
Key Points
California's Proposition 40, the Nov. 3 Election Day ballot measure, would levy a one-time, 5% "wealth tax" on residents of the state with a net worth above $1 billion, an estimated 200-250 billionaire individuals.
While polling from just a few months ago showed a significant edge for the wealth tax, more recent polling suggests the gap has narrowed, and prediction markets expect defeat.
Proponents say the measure could raise as much as $100 billion to fund healthcare in the state after significant cuts resulting from President Trump's tax act, but fears of billionaires leaving the state, highlighted this week by Mark Zuckerberg's invoking of that threat to gain a new stock plan from Meta, are among reasons some economists expect a big government revenue hit.
Opponents include Gov. Gavin Newsom, both candidates to replace him, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who is among leaders of an effort to defeat the measure, with billionaire-aligned groups spending an estimated $1 million per day.

Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/arguments-rebuttals.htm), California's billionaire tax proposal, would authorize a one-time, 5% "wealth tax" (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/21/what-to-know-about-the-billionaire-tax-on-the-ballot-in-california.html) on residents of the state with a net worth above $1 billion. The Nov. 3 Election Day ballot measure has divided politicians, the wealthy, economists, public policy groups, and voters, and it is looking more likely that the vote is headed down to the wire.
The initiative is a major test of the appetite for state-level taxation of extreme wealth — its result, economists say, could shape how other states approach wealth tax policy going forward.
What the latest polls show
In a University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted in September, 45% of likely voters said they would vote "Yes" on Proposition 40, while 42% said they would vote "No."
The results continued a recent shift (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html?eafs_enabled=false) in the pollster's data, with the "Yes" edge shrinking from 7% to 3%. In its early August survey, UC Berkeley IGS found 48% of likely voters said they would vote yes. In its polling last March, "Yes" on Prop 40 had a 19% margin, with 52% of those polled expressing support and only 33% expressing opposition. According to its September poll, 13% of voters remain undecided.
A more recent poll conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research for NBC Universal and Telemundo found "Yes" still has a sizable 10% advantage.
Large partisan differences characterize support and opposition to Proposition 40, with Democrats supporting it by more than three to one, while Republicans are opposed nearly eight to one. The views
of non-partisan voters are similar to those of the overall electorate.
While "Yes" continues to have an edge in the polls, prediction markets see Prop 40 going down to defeat by a wide margin. Both Kalshi (https://kalshi.com/markets/kxcawealthtax/will-the-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-initiative-pass/kxcawealthtax-26) and Polymarket (https://polymarket.us/event/ref-ca-blntax-2026-11-03) have the odds of passage currently at under 30%. These markets are not structured with methodologies used by traditional political polling.
How much money the measure could raise
The vast majority of the tax revenue would be used on state-funded healthcare programs, which will help offset healthcare cuts stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/08/tax-break-wealthy-investors-qsbs.html) signed into law by President Trump last year, and which is estimated by the state's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office to cost California "as much as tens of billions of dollars" though it says the impact on general funding will ultimately be determined by discretionary healthcare policy choices made by the legislature.
There are an estimated 200-250 billionaires (https://cabillionairetracker.org/) residing in California, based on tracking of Forbes data and other sources.
Alan Auerbach, economics professor at Berkeley, said the concentration of wealth among a very small number of Californians is a key sticking point of the proposal. On the estimates of around 200 individuals, he said, "Even among this number, wealth is very concentrated among the [very] wealthiest."

Squawk Box (https://www.cnbc.com/squawk-box-us/)
Proponents of the measure say it could raise roughly $100 billion (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/galle-gamage-saez-shanskeCAbillionairetaxDec25.pdf) in new tax revenue, a figure that they say also accounts for 10% of tax avoidance and evasion.
The California Budget & Policy Center, a think tank focused on the needs of low- and middle-income citizens, describes the measure (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) as one that "could potentially raise tens of billions in revenue in the short-term to preserve critical services."
That echoes the view of the state Legislative Analyst's Office, which estimates (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) that the measure would raise "tens of billions of dollars," spread over a number of years.
The authors of a study from conservative-leaning Hoover Institution, including Stanford University finance professor Joshua Rauh, estimate $30 billion in new revenue (https://www.hoover.org/research/net-present-value-california-billionaire-tax-act), factoring in migration of billionaires out of the state and future constitutional challenges. But it is their outlook for longer-term economic harm, most recently updated in an NBER research paper (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35899) published this month, that has attracted the most attention among those battling over the measure.
Concerns about billionaires fleeing California
The idea of driving the super-wealthy (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/21/campaign-against-billionaire-tax-heres-what-to-know.html) away from the state has become a major area of concern for the plan's critics, who argue that "mobility" fundamentally undermines the tax base. The estimates of tax revenue depend in part on whether billionaires are able to leave the state and avoid taxes, and how many billionaires decide to take this action.
Many have pointed to Google co-founder Sergey Brin's purchase of a Miami home in March 2026.
Auerbach acknowledged the roughly $100 billion revenue estimate advanced by supporters but cautioned that assumptions about mobility and behavioral change on the part of taxpayers are so broad in range that it is possible to arrive at revenue estimates that are "negative if one accounts for future losses in income taxes from people who will have left California."
The California Budget & Policy Center said the measure "may also lead to some income tax revenue losses in future years to the extent that billionaires leave the state to avoid the tax."
The state's nonpartisan fiscal advisor stated that there is a "possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires."
The Hoover Institution forecasts that with billionaires contributing $3.3–$5.8 billion annually in state income taxes, "permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion."
Andrew Gonzales, council representative, LA/OC Building and Construction Trades Council, speaks during a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship Training Center on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026 in La Palma, CA.
Eric Thayer | Los Angeles Times | Getty Images
One of the most vocal critics comes within Democrats' own ranks, as incumbent California Governor Gavin Newsom has frequently argued that a state-level wealth tax could weaken California's long-term tax base.
"The fight to make the wealthiest Americans pay more in taxes is not one we should be fighting state by state," Newsom said in a June Substack post (https://gavinnewsom.substack.com/p/its-time-for-a-national-billionaires). "You may not be able to pick up and move to Texas or Florida to shelter your income from taxation, but I promise you that billionaires can, and do. Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes."
Newsom, who earlier this month officially said he was a No vote on Prop 40, while a Yes vote on another measure that would bar the state from considering retroactive taxes, has also argued that the proposal could ultimately reduce funding for public services if high earners leave the state, reducing investments in needs like teachers, librarians, childcare, firefighting and police.
Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, said during a recent debate with Republican candidate Steve Hilton that "too many" California billionaires are not paying their fair share. He argued that when someone pays a lower tax rate than "a teacher, a firefighter, a nurse," they are not paying fairly. But Becerra said he will vote no on Proposition 40, because "this is not the way to do tax policy. ... What you don't do is, you don't have a policy where it's a one-time tax and it isn't predictable and sustainable," Becerra said.
"I agree that we can't drive more tax revenue out of our state, because we need that money here, and this initiative would do that," Hilton said.
