The mobility question is critical when the wealth being targeted for taxation is concentrated in financial assets that can be moved, restructured, or shielded.
One of the proposal's drafters, Darien Shanske, a law professor at UC Davis, downplays reports of wealthy Californians relocating in anticipation of the measure. "This proposal was drafted by three law professors and includes a pathway for accelerated review for some issues because we are confident in the tax's design," he said. "Given the sledgehammer that the OBBBA took to services (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/21/trump-big-beautiful-bill-tax-breaks.html) in order to pay for unneeded regressive tax cuts, it makes sense to close the loophole at least temporarily," he added.
According to Shanske, under longstanding California residency law, many highly publicized relocations may not meaningfully alter tax exposure under the proposal. Any billionaire residing in the state on January 1, 2026 would still be taxed, he said, based on longstanding Californialaw (https://ota.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/54/2021/06/18010932_Bracamonte_Opinion_P.pdf). He also argues that many lawyers who represent the wealthy (https://news.bloombergtax.com/daily-tax-report-state/billionaires-fleeing-california-to-hit-tax-officials-scrutiny) say even billionaires who bought residences outside the state before that date may face hurdles in challenging state tax law.
Shanske say some relocation rhetoric is politically strategic: "I conclude they are loudly doing these silly things in order to defeat the measure by creating doubt and confusion," he said.
But the legal and constitutional challenges that could mount in the event of the ballot measure passing are issues of significant debate, and led to a social media dustup (https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988785587925321?s=20) this week between backers of the proposal and the authors of the Hoover Institution research.
How wealth is valued
Some opposition to Prop. 40 centers as much around valuation complexity as the possibility of wealth flight.
Indeed, Prop. 40's scope of taxation applies to a mix of liquid and illiquid assets, including public equities, private business stakes, venture capital holdings, and complex ownership structures. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
"Valuing private companies and nontraded assets is an issue for any wealth tax," Auerbach said.
This issue is particularly relevant in California, where billionaire wealth is often tied to technology companies, startup equity and other illiquid assets whose valuations can fluctuate sharply and become contentious.
But Shanske says arguments that the proposal would prove administratively unworkable are unfounded.
"Most of the assets of billionaires are public and hence readily valued," Shanske said. "As for private companies, there is a default valuation formula based on the longstanding and successful formula used in Switzerland (https://kubera-equity.com/en/understanding-capitalization-rate-in-business-valuation/)," he said. "The tax can be deferred for 5 years (with a little interest) or deferred even longer if a taxpayer is truly illiquid."
Shanske says the most important point is that California's current tax structure largely fails to reach the wealthiest residents because billionaires often do not realize taxable income in the conventional sense.
"People at the very top do not pay much income tax because they do not earn much income, which is to say that, at the very top, California's progressive income tax is not progressive at all," Shanske said.
"The super wealthy do not earn much in salary, nor do they sell their assets and so they do not earn much in income. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. Billionaire tax explained: What you need to know about Prop. 40
by
Jeanne Kuang (https://calmatters.org/author/jeanne-kuang/) and Kristen Hwang (https://calmatters.org/author/kristen-hwang/)

In summary
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax on billionaires. Some say the initiative opens the door to tax flight and more aggressive taxation. Others say there’s no way to predict the outcome.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), also known as the billionaire tax, is the most contentious fight on Californians’ ballots this November.
The proposal to impose a one-time asset tax on the net worth of the state’s approximately 200 billionaires has divided Democrats, galvanized progressives and sparked fierce pushback from business groups and the state’s wealthy tech sector. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has poured $102 million into the campaign against the measure — including two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) — and is among a handful of billionaires who have moved residences or business assets out of the state in an attempt to avoid the proposed tax. In total, opponents have raised more than $205 million to stop Prop. 40, according to campaign finance records.
It would also set up an entirely new system of taxes in a state that doesn’t traditionally tax wealth. That would be challenging to implement and experts say is sure to invite litigation. Here are some common questions and answers about how the measure would work.
How would the state assess the tax?
Aside from local taxes on real estate and some business equipment, California isn’t in the business of valuing and taxing personal property.
Prop. 40 would require the state, within six months, to create a way to assess the value of a wide range of holdings: billionaires’ stock, investment accounts and business interests, but also their art collections, wine vaults, cars and anything else that stores wealth.
“I have a client who has a machine gun collection,” said Jon Feldhammer, a San Francisco tax attorney who said he is advising several clients who would be or believe they could be subject to the billionaire tax.
The definition of wealth and property has to be broad to close possible loopholes, said Kirk Stark, a UCLA tax law professor.
“Otherwise there would be a very simple workaround, which is, if there’s something that’s exempt then you know there would be an incentive to just shift wealth from one form to another,” Stark said.
Ensuring those subject to the tax aren’t underreporting their assets would require the state’s Franchise Tax Board to hire more people for appraisals and auditing, Stark said.
“It can be done,” he said. “But it’s going to take a huge investment of resources to actually pull it off.”
Franchise Tax Board spokesperson Andrew LePage declined to say how many staff the agency would need to implement Prop. 40. Currently, the board doesn’t appraise property but sometimes auditors “examine asset values reported by taxpayers to ensure accuracy,” he said.
Chris Parker, a former attorney for the tax board who now works as a tax attorney with the firm Baker Tilly, said the board has “no way of knowing anyone’s net wealth.”

Ariel Jurow Kleiman, a tax policy professor at the University of Southern California, doesn’t think the state would have a hard time putting the tax into effect. Stocks, which make up a substantial part of billionaires’ wealth, are easily valued, she said. For more “bespoke” property like art and jewelry, California could look to the Internal Revenue Service’s federal tax on inherited property.
“There are commonsense methods like looking at comparable assets or looking to available markets to see how comps are valued,” she said. “We wouldn’t be asking people to reinvent the wheel here.”
Experts do expect disputes over the value of privately held businesses.

Feldhammer said many startup founders have raised money for their companies but haven’t yet sold any products. He criticized the ballot measure for defining a company’s worth as the most recent amount of investment money it raised, which diverges from how the IRS calculates an asset’s fair market value for the estate tax.
“How do you value a company that is not on the public market? It doesn’t even have a product yet. It’s not making any money,” he said.
He said he expects clients to mount lengthy legal challenges arguing the law overvalues their business holdings.
“These are people who have oftentimes plenty of wealth to spend on legal fees to put up the best defense money can buy,” he said.
Will billionaires leave?
The campaign against the measure warns that billionaires will flee California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-unions-billionaire-tax-ballot/), depriving the state of billions of dollars in income tax revenue that helps fund the state budget. Experts say there’s no way to know whether the tax will spark a large-scale exodus.
Joel Slemrod, a University of Michigan economics professor who studies tax policy, said there’s very little evidence to gauge how billionaires could react to California’s tax, partly because the proposal is unique.
California experts considering the tax have looked at wealth taxes in European countries to try to discern the impact of Prop. 40. In 1990, 12 countries had wealth taxes. Today, only four remain. Many countries abandoned them because they were difficult and expensive to implement, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-role-and-design-of-net-wealth-taxes-in-the-oecd_9789264290303-en.html). But Slemrod said those examples are “not immediately applicable” to Prop. 40 because they differed significantly in design: Tax rates were much lower, they were intended to be permanent and the money was not earmarked for special interests.
“I wouldn’t jump from the evidence we have to California,” Slemrod said.
But one issue that could matter significantly for California, Slemrod said, is that it is much easier to move assets between states than between countries, as sometimes happened in Europe. Spain allowed its provinces to enact wealth taxes and research suggests that rich people changed residences based on tax rates. (https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article-abstract/101/2/214/58521/Relocation-of-the-Rich-Migration-in-Response-to)
Researchers at the Hoover Institution (https://www.hoover.org/research/net-present-value-billionaire-tax-act-assessment-fiscal-effects-californias-proposed), a conservative policy think tank, conducted an analysis suggesting Californians need not look at history to figure out Prop. 40’s impact. Tax flight has already happened. They estimate that billionaires representing 30% of the tax base have publicly said they have left, lowering state revenue estimates by $60 billion and permanently altering California’s income tax collection.
Feldhammer, the tax lawyer, said “a third to half” of his clients have left the state over the proposed tax. He declined to say how many clients that is. Other tax lawyers told CalMatters that clients who are worth less than $1 billion are also considering moving to avoid limiting their earning potential.
Billionaires who didn’t leave before Jan. 1 would face taxes on their assets anyway; the measure would apply to anyone who was a California resident on that date.
But Feldhammer said he expects people to sue over the measure’s retroactive nature, pointing to two U.S. Supreme Court decisions from the 1920s that held it was unconstitutional to apply the federal estate and gift taxes to assets transferred before those laws were enacted. In 1994, the court ruled that retroactive taxes could be constitutional in certain limited circumstances.
Asked how he’s advising clients who are considering leaving California, Feldhammer said there’s a “reasonable argument that the law may be unconstitutionally retroactive — but to take advantage of that, you’re going to have to leave.”
Would it allow the state to tax my retirement?
If you’re not a billionaire, no.
Even for billionaires, Prop. 40 exempts pensions and individual retirement accounts from the asset tax. There are some exceptions, most notably for Roth IRAs that contain more than $10 million.
Misleading advertisements from opponents claim the tax would allow California soon to eat into retirement savings for average Californians. They’re supporting Prop. 42, which would block the proposed billionaire tax by broadly banning any new taxes on personal property such as investment, retirement and pension accounts. Brin’s political spending group, Building a Better California, put it on the ballot, and unions representing firefighters, police and construction workers support it. (If both measures pass, (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) whichever receives more “yes” votes becomes law.)
Proponents of Prop. 42 say their measure would protect the pensions and retirement accounts of teachers, firefighters and middle-class workers from being taxed before they withdraw the money.
“A new tax on Californians’ retirement and life savings would be devastating,” Robert Gutierrez, president of the California Taxpayers Association, said in a press release.
There are no active proposals to tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature. Lawmakers who have floated such wealth taxes in the past have gotten nowhere.
Still, Brian Marvel, president of the Peace Officers Research Association of California, which supports Prop. 42, denied being deceptive and said it’s “within the realm of realization” for California to tax middle-class workers’ retirement accounts.
“I think it’s more important to be proactive in this area,” he said.
How would the money be used?
Proponents say the billionaire tax is intended to backfill federal cuts to the state’s expansive Medi-Cal health program (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/) for low-income residents. State officials project the cuts, enacted as part of President Donald Trump’s 2025 budget bill known as H.R. 1, could amount to $30 billion a year (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/the-cut-medi-cal-ripple-effects/).
The initiative gives the Legislature broad authority to decide how to spend the money. Of the revenue, 90% percent would be put in a special fund for healthcare; the other 10% would be put in a special fund to pay for schools and food assistance like CalFresh, which was also targeted by federal cuts.
If the money is used to keep Californians on Medi-Cal, that could mean spending it on the private health insurance companies that the state contracts with to administer low-income residents’ coverage.
There is some debate over whether the money would actually offset the cuts to Medi-Cal and how strictly the language bars lawmakers from using the money for anything else.
Opponents such as the California Medical Association and Planned Parenthood recently circulated a memo (https://calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Memo_Health-Care-Funding-Under-Prop-40_9.18.26.pdf) arguing there’s no guarantee the money would replace the federal funding cuts, because the proposition also allows the money to offset state cuts to Medi-Cal. They warn that would allow lawmakers and the governor to use the new tax money to maintain state funding levels for Medi-Cal and free up the state’s general fund to pay for other things.
Lawmakers and governors have in the past used special new funds to simply replace existing funding. Then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, did it with mental health funding created by a voter-approved tax on millionaires, and then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, did it with health funding created by the state tobacco tax. More recently, doctors and hospitals accused Newsom of using a different healthcare tax to backfill the general fund. They placed Proposition 35 on the ballot in 2024 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/11/election-result-proposition-35/) to earmark the money. Voters approved it, but the groups say some funding was still diverted.
But proponents of Prop. 40 said that concern doesn’t make sense: Those budget maneuvers, they said, are usually done to address state budget shortfalls, while Prop. 40 was already written to create funding for a shortfall.
For the record: This story has been updated to correct the amount that Brin has donated to a political action committee opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Props. 41 and 42. He has donated $102 million.

Top 10 Contributors List
In 2014, the Fair Political Practices Commission began posting lists of the top 10 contributors to committees primarily formed to support or oppose state ballot measures and independent expenditure committees supporting or opposing state candidates that raised at least a million dollars. These lists help voters cut through the noise by providing a snapshot of the top funders for various campaigns. Click on one of the following links below to see the results:
Overview of November 2026 General Election (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/)
Overview of June 2026 Primary Election (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/june-2026-primary-election/)
How it Works
Committees are required to submit a Form T10 (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/siteassets/documents/tad/forms/campaign/t10.pdf) (or Form T10 Excel (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/siteassets/documents/tad/t10/Form-t10-spreadsheet-excel.xlsx)) detailing their top contributors to the FPPC. Any time a change occurs in the list (e.g. additional contributions, a new contributor, or a change in the relative ordering of the contributors) committees are required to submit a new list to the FPPC to be posted on its website.
Committees Required to Report
Two types of committees are required to report their top contributors to the FPPC:
Committees that raise $1,000,000 or more and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state ballot measure.
Committees that raise $1,000,000 or more and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state candidate.
General purpose committees (commonly referred to as PACs) and committees controlled by a state candidate for their own election are not required to submit their top contributors to the FPPC. However, the California Secretary of State's campaign finance database (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/) provides comprehensive data on any state committee's donors.
Additional Information
For a detailed explanation of how the top contributor lists are created as well as the statutory and regulatory provisions that govern the process, please read Methodology and Legal Resources (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/methodology-and-legal-resources/).

Top 10 Contributors List
In 2014, the Fair Political Practices Commission began posting lists of the top 10 contributors to committees primarily formed to support or oppose state ballot measures and independent expenditure committees supporting or opposing state candidates that raised at least a million dollars. These lists help voters cut through the noise by providing a snapshot of the top funders for various campaigns. Click on one of the following links below to see the results:
Overview of November 2026 General Election (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/)
Overview of June 2026 Primary Election (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/june-2026-primary-election/)
How it Works
Committees are required to submit a Form T10 (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/siteassets/documents/tad/forms/campaign/t10.pdf) (or Form T10 Excel (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/siteassets/documents/tad/t10/Form-t10-spreadsheet-excel.xlsx)) detailing their top contributors to the FPPC. Any time a change occurs in the list (e.g. additional contributions, a new contributor, or a change in the relative ordering of the contributors) committees are required to submit a new list to the FPPC to be posted on its website.
Committees Required to Report
Two types of committees are required to report their top contributors to the FPPC:
Committees that raise $1,000,000 or more and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state ballot measure.
Committees that raise $1,000,000 or more and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state candidate.
General purpose committees (commonly referred to as PACs) and committees controlled by a state candidate for their own election are not required to submit their top contributors to the FPPC. However, the California Secretary of State's campaign finance database (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/) provides comprehensive data on any state committee's donors.
Additional Information
For a detailed explanation of how the top contributor lists are created as well as the statutory and regulatory provisions that govern the process, please read Methodology and Legal Resources (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/methodology-and-legal-resources/).

Top 10 Contributors List
In 2014, the Fair Political Practices Commission began posting lists of the top 10 contributors to committees primarily formed to support or oppose state ballot measures and independent expenditure committees supporting or opposing state candidates that raised at least a million dollars. These lists help voters cut through the noise by providing a snapshot of the top funders for various campaigns. Click on one of the following links below to see the results:
Overview of November 2026 General Election (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/)
Overview of June 2026 Primary Election (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/june-2026-primary-election/)
How it Works
Committees are required to submit a Form T10 (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/siteassets/documents/tad/forms/campaign/t10.pdf) (or Form T10 Excel (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/siteassets/documents/tad/t10/Form-t10-spreadsheet-excel.xlsx)) detailing their top contributors to the FPPC. Any time a change occurs in the list (e.g. additional contributions, a new contributor, or a change in the relative ordering of the contributors) committees are required to submit a new list to the FPPC to be posted on its website.
Committees Required to Report
Two types of committees are required to report their top contributors to the FPPC:
Committees that raise $1,000,000 or more and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state ballot measure.
Committees that raise $1,000,000 or more and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state candidate.
General purpose committees (commonly referred to as PACs) and committees controlled by a state candidate for their own election are not required to submit their top contributors to the FPPC. However, the California Secretary of State's campaign finance database (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/) provides comprehensive data on any state committee's donors.
Additional Information
For a detailed explanation of how the top contributor lists are created as well as the statutory and regulatory provisions that govern the process, please read Methodology and Legal Resources (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/methodology-and-legal-resources/).

The Fair Political Practices Commission is a five-member independent, non-partisan commission that has primary responsibility for the impartial and effective administration of the Political Reform Act.
The Act regulates campaign financing, conflicts of interest, lobbying, and governmental ethics. The Commission's objectives are to ensure that public officials act in a fair and unbiased manner in the governmental decision-making process, to promote transparency in government, and to foster public trust in the political system.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.

Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

PROP 42: The Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-09/California%20Decides_Proposition%2042.pdf)
Research
Overview
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Proposition 42 would add a new article to the California Constitution with two main provisions:
First, it would prohibit any new taxes on personal property—both tangible (i.e., personal belongings) and intangible (savings, retirement accounts, financial assets, business ownership, intellectual property, etc.)—while leaving existing property taxes untouched. In effect, this would require that the California legislature get voters’ approval before creating any new property taxes.
Second, it would prohibit new taxes that impose liability for past residency or conduct, with a narrow exception allowing taxes to reach back up to 365 days if tied to a governor-declared emergency and dedicated to addressing it.
Notably, if Prop 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, it would nullify Prop 40 entirely. Given the two propositions fundamentally conflict, this kind of specificity is valuable to clearly determine what happens after the election. This is arguably the most relevant element of Prop 42, because Prop 40 could possibly allow future legislators to pass new taxes on personal property.
Fellows at the Hoover Institution have extensively researched (https://fiscalrealitycheck.substack.com/p/a-california-ballot-collision-wealth) Prop 40, Prop 42, and California’s fiscal problems more generally. The biggest fiscal challenge the state faces is an exuberance of spending beyond what even its rapidly increasing tax revenue can sustain.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0041A1)
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment and statute
A vote YES means: A prohibition on new state taxes on personal property, including financial assets. Retroactive taxes would be prohibited except during a state of emergency. If Proposition 42 outpolls Proposition 40, it would specifically void Prop 40 (see California Decides Proposition Lab, Prop 40: The Billionaire Tax Act (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)).
A vote NO means: The legislature would not be forbidden from passing new taxes on personal property, including financial assets. The legislature would not be forbidden from passing retroactive taxes. The lack of these restrictions is especially relevant if Proposition 40 passes, because Prop 40 arguably empowers future legislatures to pass new taxes on personal property and to create retroactive taxes.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0041A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0041A1%20(Retirement%20Protection%20).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0041 (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250545.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 40 imposes a one-time tax of 5 percent on the total net worth of any California resident worth $1 billion or more. The rate applies to the whole fortune, not just the amount above the threshold. A narrow phase-in ramps the rate between 0 percent at $1.0 billion and 5 percent at $1.1 billion. A married couple is treated as a single taxpayer.
Residency is set as of January 1, 2026, called the tax obligation date, and net worth is measured on December 31, 2026, called the valuation date. The January date is already in the past. A billionaire who leaves California before the election would still owe the tax if voters approve it because the law reaches back to who lived here on the first day of the year. The tax is due in 2027 with 2026 tax returns, payable in full or in five annual installments that carry a 7.5 percent additional charge each year.
Not all assets are included in the net worth calculation. Directly held real estate is excluded, which sidesteps a fight with Proposition 13 restrictions. Pensions and traditional retirement accounts are excluded, Roth accounts are excluded up to $10 million, and up to $5 million of art, cars, and personal property is excluded.

Rauh have described how this causes substantial volatility in the California state budget (https://www.hoover.org/research/california-state-budget-and-revenue-volatility-fiscal-health-deficit-context) because most personal income tax revenue comes from high-income and high-net-worth households and tends to fluctuate with stock market performance. During the strong stock market returns in 2021 the top 10 percent of taxpayers paid almost 90 percent of personal income tax revenue.
The top 1 percent of income tax filers typically pay 40–50 percent of personal income tax revenue.
The top 0.1 percent—just twenty-five thousand households—typically pay more than 20 percent of all personal income tax revenue.

The bust should have been expected given California’s previous experience, but Governor Newsom’s administration assumed that the increased revenue would be permanent and increased government spending commensurately, leading to a $175 billion swing (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-01-27/california-budget-deficit-surplus-spending-commitments) from budget surplus to deficit just two years later.
The boom-bust nature of California’s tax revenue shows the need for better methods to smooth revenues and spending over time. Proposition 42 doesn’t change any current taxes. It effectively only adds the requirement that voters be consulted before the state creates any new property taxes. This provides high-income and high-net-worth households a credible signal that California will not—without reasonable warning—tax the ownership of personal property, especially financial assets. This could help slow the out-migration that erodes the state’s narrow, top-heavy tax base.
Prop 42 also contains a clause that if it outpolls Proposition 40, it will fully nullify Prop 40. This specificity is likely preferrable to having the courts attempt to determine which elements of Prop 40 (if any) still hold if Prop 42 has greater support.
Hoover Institution research shows that California’s spending has risen far faster than inflation or population growth, and even faster than the surprising increases in tax revenue. California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Proposition 42 would add a new article to the California Constitution with two main provisions:
First, it would prohibit any new taxes on personal property—both tangible (i.e., personal belongings) and intangible (savings, retirement accounts, financial assets, business ownership, intellectual property, etc.)—while leaving existing property taxes untouched. In effect, this would require that the California legislature get voters’ approval before creating any new property taxes.
Second, it would prohibit new taxes that impose liability for past residency or conduct, with a narrow exception allowing taxes to reach back up to 365 days if tied to a governor-declared emergency and dedicated to addressing it.
Notably, if Prop 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, it would nullify Prop 40 entirely. Given the two propositions fundamentally conflict, this kind of specificity is valuable to clearly determine what happens after the election. This is arguably the most relevant element of Prop 42, because Prop 40 could possibly allow future legislators to pass new taxes on personal property.
Fellows at the Hoover Institution have extensively researched (https://fiscalrealitycheck.substack.com/p/a-california-ballot-collision-wealth) Prop 40, Prop 42, and California’s fiscal problems more generally. The biggest fiscal challenge the state faces is an exuberance of spending beyond what even its rapidly increasing tax revenue can sustain.

A vote NO means: The legislature would not be forbidden from passing new taxes on personal property, including financial assets. The legislature would not be forbidden from passing retroactive taxes. The lack of these restrictions is especially relevant if Proposition 40 passes, because Prop 40 arguably empowers future legislatures to pass new taxes on personal property and to create retroactive taxes.

The Bottom Line (https://www.cnbc.com/global-cfo-council/) California's Proposition 40: What voters need to know about billionaire wealth tax battle
Published Thu, Oct 22 2026 8:05 AM EDT Updated Thu, Oct 22 2026 12:04 PM EDT
Trevor Laurence Jockims (https://www.cnbc.com/trevor-laurence-jockims/)
WATCH LIVE (https://www.cnbc.com/live-tv/)
Key Points
California's Proposition 40, the Nov. 3 Election Day ballot measure, would levy a one-time, 5% "wealth tax" on residents of the state with a net worth above $1 billion, an estimated 200-250 billionaire individuals.
While polling from just a few months ago showed a significant edge for the wealth tax, more recent polling suggests the gap has narrowed, and prediction markets expect defeat.
Proponents say the measure could raise as much as $100 billion to fund healthcare in the state after significant cuts resulting from President Trump's tax act, but fears of billionaires leaving the state, highlighted this week by Mark Zuckerberg's invoking of that threat to gain a new stock plan from Meta, are among reasons some economists expect a big government revenue hit.
Opponents include Gov. Gavin Newsom, both candidates to replace him, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who is among leaders of an effort to defeat the measure, with billionaire-aligned groups spending an estimated $1 million per day.

Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/arguments-rebuttals.htm), California's billionaire tax proposal, would authorize a one-time, 5% "wealth tax" (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/21/what-to-know-about-the-billionaire-tax-on-the-ballot-in-california.html) on residents of the state with a net worth above $1 billion. The Nov. 3 Election Day ballot measure has divided politicians, the wealthy, economists, public policy groups, and voters, and it is looking more likely that the vote is headed down to the wire.
The initiative is a major test of the appetite for state-level taxation of extreme wealth — its result, economists say, could shape how other states approach wealth tax policy going forward.
What the latest polls show
In a University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted in September, 45% of likely voters said they would vote "Yes" on Proposition 40, while 42% said they would vote "No."
The results continued a recent shift (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html?eafs_enabled=false) in the pollster's data, with the "Yes" edge shrinking from 7% to 3%. In its early August survey, UC Berkeley IGS found 48% of likely voters said they would vote yes. In its polling last March, "Yes" on Prop 40 had a 19% margin, with 52% of those polled expressing support and only 33% expressing opposition. According to its September poll, 13% of voters remain undecided.
A more recent poll conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research for NBC Universal and Telemundo found "Yes" still has a sizable 10% advantage.
Large partisan differences characterize support and opposition to Proposition 40, with Democrats supporting it by more than three to one, while Republicans are opposed nearly eight to one. The views
of non-partisan voters are similar to those of the overall electorate.
While "Yes" continues to have an edge in the polls, prediction markets see Prop 40 going down to defeat by a wide margin. Both Kalshi (https://kalshi.com/markets/kxcawealthtax/will-the-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-initiative-pass/kxcawealthtax-26) and Polymarket (https://polymarket.us/event/ref-ca-blntax-2026-11-03) have the odds of passage currently at under 30%. These markets are not structured with methodologies used by traditional political polling.
How much money the measure could raise
The vast majority of the tax revenue would be used on state-funded healthcare programs, which will help offset healthcare cuts stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/08/tax-break-wealthy-investors-qsbs.html) signed into law by President Trump last year, and which is estimated by the state's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office to cost California "as much as tens of billions of dollars" though it says the impact on general funding will ultimately be determined by discretionary healthcare policy choices made by the legislature.
There are an estimated 200-250 billionaires (https://cabillionairetracker.org/) residing in California, based on tracking of Forbes data and other sources.
Alan Auerbach, economics professor at Berkeley, said the concentration of wealth among a very small number of Californians is a key sticking point of the proposal. On the estimates of around 200 individuals, he said, "Even among this number, wealth is very concentrated among the [very] wealthiest."

Squawk Box (https://www.cnbc.com/squawk-box-us/)
Proponents of the measure say it could raise roughly $100 billion (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/galle-gamage-saez-shanskeCAbillionairetaxDec25.pdf) in new tax revenue, a figure that they say also accounts for 10% of tax avoidance and evasion.
The California Budget & Policy Center, a think tank focused on the needs of low- and middle-income citizens, describes the measure (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) as one that "could potentially raise tens of billions in revenue in the short-term to preserve critical services."
That echoes the view of the state Legislative Analyst's Office, which estimates (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) that the measure would raise "tens of billions of dollars," spread over a number of years.
The authors of a study from conservative-leaning Hoover Institution, including Stanford University finance professor Joshua Rauh, estimate $30 billion in new revenue (https://www.hoover.org/research/net-present-value-california-billionaire-tax-act), factoring in migration of billionaires out of the state and future constitutional challenges. But it is their outlook for longer-term economic harm, most recently updated in an NBER research paper (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35899) published this month, that has attracted the most attention among those battling over the measure.
Concerns about billionaires fleeing California
The idea of driving the super-wealthy (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/21/campaign-against-billionaire-tax-heres-what-to-know.html) away from the state has become a major area of concern for the plan's critics, who argue that "mobility" fundamentally undermines the tax base. The estimates of tax revenue depend in part on whether billionaires are able to leave the state and avoid taxes, and how many billionaires decide to take this action.
Many have pointed to Google co-founder Sergey Brin's purchase of a Miami home in March 2026.
Auerbach acknowledged the roughly $100 billion revenue estimate advanced by supporters but cautioned that assumptions about mobility and behavioral change on the part of taxpayers are so broad in range that it is possible to arrive at revenue estimates that are "negative if one accounts for future losses in income taxes from people who will have left California."
The California Budget & Policy Center said the measure "may also lead to some income tax revenue losses in future years to the extent that billionaires leave the state to avoid the tax."
The state's nonpartisan fiscal advisor stated that there is a "possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires."
The Hoover Institution forecasts that with billionaires contributing $3.3–$5.8 billion annually in state income taxes, "permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion."
Andrew Gonzales, council representative, LA/OC Building and Construction Trades Council, speaks during a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship Training Center on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026 in La Palma, CA.
Eric Thayer | Los Angeles Times | Getty Images
One of the most vocal critics comes within Democrats' own ranks, as incumbent California Governor Gavin Newsom has frequently argued that a state-level wealth tax could weaken California's long-term tax base.
"The fight to make the wealthiest Americans pay more in taxes is not one we should be fighting state by state," Newsom said in a June Substack post (https://gavinnewsom.substack.com/p/its-time-for-a-national-billionaires). "You may not be able to pick up and move to Texas or Florida to shelter your income from taxation, but I promise you that billionaires can, and do. Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes."
Newsom, who earlier this month officially said he was a No vote on Prop 40, while a Yes vote on another measure that would bar the state from considering retroactive taxes, has also argued that the proposal could ultimately reduce funding for public services if high earners leave the state, reducing investments in needs like teachers, librarians, childcare, firefighting and police.
Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, said during a recent debate with Republican candidate Steve Hilton that "too many" California billionaires are not paying their fair share. He argued that when someone pays a lower tax rate than "a teacher, a firefighter, a nurse," they are not paying fairly. But Becerra said he will vote no on Proposition 40, because "this is not the way to do tax policy. ... What you don't do is, you don't have a policy where it's a one-time tax and it isn't predictable and sustainable," Becerra said.
"I agree that we can't drive more tax revenue out of our state, because we need that money here, and this initiative would do that," Hilton said.

The mobility question is critical when the wealth being targeted for taxation is concentrated in financial assets that can be moved, restructured, or shielded.
One of the proposal's drafters, Darien Shanske, a law professor at UC Davis, downplays reports of wealthy Californians relocating in anticipation of the measure. "This proposal was drafted by three law professors and includes a pathway for accelerated review for some issues because we are confident in the tax's design," he said. "Given the sledgehammer that the OBBBA took to services (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/21/trump-big-beautiful-bill-tax-breaks.html) in order to pay for unneeded regressive tax cuts, it makes sense to close the loophole at least temporarily," he added.
According to Shanske, under longstanding California residency law, many highly publicized relocations may not meaningfully alter tax exposure under the proposal. Any billionaire residing in the state on January 1, 2026 would still be taxed, he said, based on longstanding Californialaw (https://ota.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/54/2021/06/18010932_Bracamonte_Opinion_P.pdf). He also argues that many lawyers who represent the wealthy (https://news.bloombergtax.com/daily-tax-report-state/billionaires-fleeing-california-to-hit-tax-officials-scrutiny) say even billionaires who bought residences outside the state before that date may face hurdles in challenging state tax law.
Shanske say some relocation rhetoric is politically strategic: "I conclude they are loudly doing these silly things in order to defeat the measure by creating doubt and confusion," he said.
But the legal and constitutional challenges that could mount in the event of the ballot measure passing are issues of significant debate, and led to a social media dustup (https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988785587925321?s=20) this week between backers of the proposal and the authors of the Hoover Institution research.
How wealth is valued
Some opposition to Prop. 40 centers as much around valuation complexity as the possibility of wealth flight.
Indeed, Prop. 40's scope of taxation applies to a mix of liquid and illiquid assets, including public equities, private business stakes, venture capital holdings, and complex ownership structures. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
"Valuing private companies and nontraded assets is an issue for any wealth tax," Auerbach said.
This issue is particularly relevant in California, where billionaire wealth is often tied to technology companies, startup equity and other illiquid assets whose valuations can fluctuate sharply and become contentious.
But Shanske says arguments that the proposal would prove administratively unworkable are unfounded.
"Most of the assets of billionaires are public and hence readily valued," Shanske said. "As for private companies, there is a default valuation formula based on the longstanding and successful formula used in Switzerland (https://kubera-equity.com/en/understanding-capitalization-rate-in-business-valuation/)," he said. "The tax can be deferred for 5 years (with a little interest) or deferred even longer if a taxpayer is truly illiquid."
Shanske says the most important point is that California's current tax structure largely fails to reach the wealthiest residents because billionaires often do not realize taxable income in the conventional sense.
"People at the very top do not pay much income tax because they do not earn much income, which is to say that, at the very top, California's progressive income tax is not progressive at all," Shanske said.
"The super wealthy do not earn much in salary, nor do they sell their assets and so they do not earn much in income. A more recent poll conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research for NBC Universal and Telemundo found "Yes" still has a sizable 10% advantage.
Large partisan differences characterize support and opposition to Proposition 40, with Democrats supporting it by more than three to one, while Republicans are opposed nearly eight to one. The views
of non-partisan voters are similar to those of the overall electorate.
While "Yes" continues to have an edge in the polls, prediction markets see Prop 40 going down to defeat by a wide margin. Both Kalshi (https://kalshi.com/markets/kxcawealthtax/will-the-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-initiative-pass/kxcawealthtax-26) and Polymarket (https://polymarket.us/event/ref-ca-blntax-2026-11-03) have the odds of passage currently at under 30%. These markets are not structured with methodologies used by traditional political polling.
How much money the measure could raise
The vast majority of the tax revenue would be used on state-funded healthcare programs, which will help offset healthcare cuts stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/08/tax-break-wealthy-investors-qsbs.html) signed into law by President Trump last year, and which is estimated by the state's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office to cost California "as much as tens of billions of dollars" though it says the impact on general funding will ultimately be determined by discretionary healthcare policy choices made by the legislature.
There are an estimated 200-250 billionaires (https://cabillionairetracker.org/) residing in California, based on tracking of Forbes data and other sources.
Alan Auerbach, economics professor at Berkeley, said the concentration of wealth among a very small number of Californians is a key sticking point of the proposal. On the estimates of around 200 individuals, he said, "Even among this number, wealth is very concentrated among the [very] wealthiest."

Squawk Box (https://www.cnbc.com/squawk-box-us/)
Proponents of the measure say it could raise roughly $100 billion (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/galle-gamage-saez-shanskeCAbillionairetaxDec25.pdf) in new tax revenue, a figure that they say also accounts for 10% of tax avoidance and evasion.
The California Budget & Policy Center, a think tank focused on the needs of low- and middle-income citizens, describes the measure (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) as one that "could potentially raise tens of billions in revenue in the short-term to preserve critical services."
That echoes the view of the state Legislative Analyst's Office, which estimates (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) that the measure would raise "tens of billions of dollars," spread over a number of years.
The authors of a study from conservative-leaning Hoover Institution, including Stanford University finance professor Joshua Rauh, estimate $30 billion in new revenue (https://www.hoover.org/research/net-present-value-california-billionaire-tax-act), factoring in migration of billionaires out of the state and future constitutional challenges. But it is their outlook for longer-term economic harm, most recently updated in an NBER research paper (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35899) published this month, that has attracted the most attention among those battling over the measure.
Concerns about billionaires fleeing California
The idea of driving the super-wealthy (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/21/campaign-against-billionaire-tax-heres-what-to-know.html) away from the state has become a major area of concern for the plan's critics, who argue that "mobility" fundamentally undermines the tax base. The estimates of tax revenue depend in part on whether billionaires are able to leave the state and avoid taxes, and how many billionaires decide to take this action.
Many have pointed to Google co-founder Sergey Brin's purchase of a Miami home in March 2026.
Auerbach acknowledged the roughly $100 billion revenue estimate advanced by supporters but cautioned that assumptions about mobility and behavioral change on the part of taxpayers are so broad in range that it is possible to arrive at revenue estimates that are "negative if one accounts for future losses in income taxes from people who will have left California."
The California Budget & Policy Center said the measure "may also lead to some income tax revenue losses in future years to the extent that billionaires leave the state to avoid the tax."
The state's nonpartisan fiscal advisor stated that there is a "possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires."
The Hoover Institution forecasts that with billionaires contributing $3.3–$5.8 billion annually in state income taxes, "permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion."
Andrew Gonzales, council representative, LA/OC Building and Construction Trades Council, speaks during a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship Training Center on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026 in La Palma, CA.
Eric Thayer | Los Angeles Times | Getty Images
One of the most vocal critics comes within Democrats' own ranks, as incumbent California Governor Gavin Newsom has frequently argued that a state-level wealth tax could weaken California's long-term tax base.
"The fight to make the wealthiest Americans pay more in taxes is not one we should be fighting state by state," Newsom said in a June Substack post (https://gavinnewsom.substack.com/p/its-time-for-a-national-billionaires). "You may not be able to pick up and move to Texas or Florida to shelter your income from taxation, but I promise you that billionaires can, and do. Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes."
Newsom, who earlier this month officially said he was a No vote on Prop 40, while a Yes vote on another measure that would bar the state from considering retroactive taxes, has also argued that the proposal could ultimately reduce funding for public services if high earners leave the state, reducing investments in needs like teachers, librarians, childcare, firefighting and police.
Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, said during a recent debate with Republican candidate Steve Hilton that "too many" California billionaires are not paying their fair share. He argued that when someone pays a lower tax rate than "a teacher, a firefighter, a nurse," they are not paying fairly. But Becerra said he will vote no on Proposition 40, because "this is not the way to do tax policy. ... What you don't do is, you don't have a policy where it's a one-time tax and it isn't predictable and sustainable," Becerra said.
"I agree that we can't drive more tax revenue out of our state, because we need that money here, and this initiative would do that," Hilton said.

The mobility question is critical when the wealth being targeted for taxation is concentrated in financial assets that can be moved, restructured, or shielded.
One of the proposal's drafters, Darien Shanske, a law professor at UC Davis, downplays reports of wealthy Californians relocating in anticipation of the measure. "This proposal was drafted by three law professors and includes a pathway for accelerated review for some issues because we are confident in the tax's design," he said. "Given the sledgehammer that the OBBBA took to services (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/21/trump-big-beautiful-bill-tax-breaks.html) in order to pay for unneeded regressive tax cuts, it makes sense to close the loophole at least temporarily," he added.
According to Shanske, under longstanding California residency law, many highly publicized relocations may not meaningfully alter tax exposure under the proposal. Any billionaire residing in the state on January 1, 2026 would still be taxed, he said, based on longstanding Californialaw (https://ota.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/54/2021/06/18010932_Bracamonte_Opinion_P.pdf). He also argues that many lawyers who represent the wealthy (https://news.bloombergtax.com/daily-tax-report-state/billionaires-fleeing-california-to-hit-tax-officials-scrutiny) say even billionaires who bought residences outside the state before that date may face hurdles in challenging state tax law.
Shanske say some relocation rhetoric is politically strategic: "I conclude they are loudly doing these silly things in order to defeat the measure by creating doubt and confusion," he said.
But the legal and constitutional challenges that could mount in the event of the ballot measure passing are issues of significant debate, and led to a social media dustup (https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988785587925321?s=20) this week between backers of the proposal and the authors of the Hoover Institution research.
How wealth is valued
Some opposition to Prop. 40 centers as much around valuation complexity as the possibility of wealth flight.
Indeed, Prop. 40's scope of taxation applies to a mix of liquid and illiquid assets, including public equities, private business stakes, venture capital holdings, and complex ownership structures. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
"Valuing private companies and nontraded assets is an issue for any wealth tax," Auerbach said.
This issue is particularly relevant in California, where billionaire wealth is often tied to technology companies, startup equity and other illiquid assets whose valuations can fluctuate sharply and become contentious.
But Shanske says arguments that the proposal would prove administratively unworkable are unfounded.
"Most of the assets of billionaires are public and hence readily valued," Shanske said. "As for private companies, there is a default valuation formula based on the longstanding and successful formula used in Switzerland (https://kubera-equity.com/en/understanding-capitalization-rate-in-business-valuation/)," he said. "The tax can be deferred for 5 years (with a little interest) or deferred even longer if a taxpayer is truly illiquid."
Shanske says the most important point is that California's current tax structure largely fails to reach the wealthiest residents because billionaires often do not realize taxable income in the conventional sense.
"People at the very top do not pay much income tax because they do not earn much income, which is to say that, at the very top, California's progressive income tax is not progressive at all," Shanske said.
"The super wealthy do not earn much in salary, nor do they sell their assets and so they do not earn much in income. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters.
